01.event: Throughout Rav Huna's lifetime, Rav Hisda was asked whether an egg may be cooked in kutah and refused to rule.
01.outcome: He never issued the ruling while his teacher lived.
01.summary: Rav Yosef told Abaye that during all the years Rav Huna was alive, his disciple Rav Hisda would not even answer a simple question about cooking an egg in a dairy dish, out of deference to his teacher's authority. It is cited as precedent rather than told as a single episode.
01.missing: A specific occasion; this reads as a standing practice rather than one event with a turn.

03.event: A bill of divorce dated by the years of the governor of Bascar came up, and Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda sent the question to Rabba.
03.turn: Rabba answered that even Rabbi Meir, who is strict about dating, would accept it, because the governor belongs to the ruling kingdom.
03.outcome: The bill of divorce was ruled valid.
03.summary: A bill of divorce turned up whose date was written by the years of the governor of Bascar rather than the king. Unsure whether it was valid, Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda sent the case to Rabba. Rabba replied that even Rabbi Meir would accept it, since the governor is an official of the same kingdom, and the document stood.

04.event: While Rabbi Yehuda and others sat before Rabbi Tarfon, a yevama came to perform halitza.
04.turn: Rabbi Tarfon told all those present to call out 'He who had his shoe removed' three times.
04.outcome: The students joined in the declaration at the ceremony.
04.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalled that once, while he and others were sitting before Rabbi Tarfon, a widow came to perform the halitza ceremony. Rabbi Tarfon instructed everyone present, not just the judges, to call out three times 'He who had his shoe removed.'
04.missing: The text does not state explicitly that they did so, only the instruction.

06.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Sages
06.event: In Rabbi's days the Sages sought to permit the Gibeonites to marry into the community.
06.turn: Rabbi objected that even if they could release the people's share, no one could release the altar's share.
06.summary: In the time of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the Sages wanted to lift the ban on the Gibeonites and let them marry fellow Jews. Rabbi stopped them: the court might waive the nation's claim on them, but who could waive the claim of the altar they had been assigned to serve?
06.missing: The outcome is implied by Rabbi's objection, not stated.

07.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Dabil; Shmuel
07.event: Rav Yosef issued a practical ruling following Rav's opinion on a father's betrothal of his daughter.
07.turn: Shmuel took offense and sarcastically asked whether wisdom had been measured out to this man in a larger measure than everyone else.
07.summary: Rav Yosef of Dabil decided an actual case according to Rav's view, against Shmuel's. Shmuel was offended and mocked him, asking whether he alone had been given a bigger portion of wisdom than everyone else. The incident is cited inside a legal argument about whether Rav and Shmuel truly disagreed.
07.missing: The details of the case and any consequence of Shmuel's rebuke.

08.event: Rav saw his uncle Rabbi Hiyya conduct halitza with a laced sandal.
08.outcome: Because of that, Rav did not limit himself to the tighter Arab sandal.
08.summary: Rav said that had he not seen his uncle Rabbi Hiyya conduct a halitza ceremony using a laced sandal, he would only ever have used the tight-fitting sandal of the Arabs. The sighting shaped his own practice.
08.missing: It is a recollection supporting a ruling rather than an episode with its own turn.

09.actor: Rabbi Elazar and an elder of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's court
09.event: Rabbi Elazar asked an elder who had been present at a case whether the court had let a woman remarry immediately or only after twelve months.
09.summary: Rabbi Elazar asked an old man who had sat on Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's court about a past case of a conditional divorce: when they allowed the widow to remarry, was it right away or only after the twelve months of the condition had passed? The text gives only the question.
09.missing: The original case and the elder's answer.

10.event: Levi publicly taught Rabbi's ruling that a bill of divorce written on forbidden-benefit items is valid, in Rabbi's name.
10.turn: The audience did not praise him; when he taught it as the majority's view, they praised him.
10.outcome: The ruling was received, showing the halakha follows it.
10.summary: Levi went out and taught that a divorce document written on material one may not benefit from is valid, citing Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. The listeners were unimpressed. He taught it again as the view of the majority, and this time they praised him.

11.actor: A debtor, his creditor, and a purchaser
11.event: A man owing 100 dinars sold two plots for 50 each; the creditor seized one and came to seize the other.
11.turn: The purchaser brought 100 dinars and told the creditor to either accept the plot as worth 100 or take the cash and give up both plots.
11.summary: A man owed a creditor 100 dinars and sold his two small fields for 50 each. The creditor took one field from the buyer, then came back for the second. The buyer showed up with 100 dinars and offered: count the field as worth 100, or take this money and leave me both fields.
11.missing: The creditor's response or the court's ruling; only later legal discussion follows.

12.actor: Two men slurred as children of Arameans; Rav Asi; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
12.event: People called one man 'son of the Aramean woman' and another 'son of an Aramean man', doubting their parents' conversions.
12.turn: Rav Asi and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi each pointed out that the parent had immersed for ritual purity, which counts as conversion.
12.summary: A man was taunted as the son of an Aramean woman, implying his mother's conversion was invalid; Rav Asi answered that she had surely immersed after menstruation, which suffices. In a similar case, a man called the son of an Aramean man was defended by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who noted that his father had immersed after a seminal emission.
12.missing: The outcome is implied by the rulings rather than narrated.

13.actor: The Sages, Rav, Shmuel and Karna
13.event: Faced with Shmuel's ruling that a minor betrothed without her father's consent needs both divorce and refusal, and Karna's objection, the Sages sent the question to Rav with the two names swapped.
13.turn: Rav, thinking Shmuel held the lenient view, swore by God that she needs both and that Shmuel could never say otherwise.
13.outcome: Rav's oath unwittingly confirmed Shmuel's actual ruling.
13.summary: Shmuel ruled that a girl betrothed without her father's consent needs both a divorce and a refusal; Karna called this self-contradictory. The Sages took the question to Rav but switched whose opinion was whose. Rav swore that she needs both, and that God forbid Shmuel should say anything else, so he ended up backing Shmuel's real position.

15.actor: A son sent by his father
15.event: A father told his son to climb a building and bring him chicks; the son sent away the mother bird and took the young.
15.turn: On the way down he fell and died, despite performing two mitzvot promised long life.
15.outcome: He died, and the rabbis concluded the promised reward refers to the World-to-Come.
15.summary: A father asked his son to climb up and fetch him some chicks. The son climbed, sent off the mother bird as the Torah requires, and took the young, keeping both commandments that promise long life. Coming down, he fell and was killed, which led Rabbi Ya'akov to teach that their reward is paid in the next world.

16.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva
16.event: The four Sages were sailing from Pelandarsin when their boat set out to sea on Shabbat.
16.turn: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar walked the whole boat, while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva would not move beyond four cubits.
16.outcome: The two pairs held to different practices for the voyage, the latter by choosing strictness.
16.summary: Four great Sages were returning from Pelandarsin when their ship sailed out on Shabbat, carrying them past their permitted boundary. Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya walked freely about the ship. Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva stayed within four cubits, choosing to be strict with themselves.

17.actor: Rav Aha son of Rav Avya
17.event: Rav Aha met Rav Ashi's students and asked whether their teacher had said anything about the form of a doorway.
17.outcome: They told him Rav Ashi said nothing at all.
17.summary: Rav Aha, son of Rav Avya, came upon some of Rav Ashi's students and asked whether their master had said anything about the 'form of a doorway' used for an eruv. They replied that he had said nothing.
17.missing: Any turn or consequence; it is a brief exchange reporting a teaching.

18.actor: The son of Nehunya the well digger
18.event: Despite his father's merit in digging wells, Nehunya's son died of thirst.
18.turn: His father's merit did not protect him, which the rabbis explain by God being exacting with the righteous.
18.summary: Rabbi Abba reported that even though Nehunya dug wells for the public, his own son died of thirst. The rabbis take this as proof that God holds those closest to Him to a hair's-breadth standard.
18.missing: Who Nehunya was and the preceding story about his daughter, which lies before segment [1]; the death is reported without circumstances.

19.event: A heretic taunted Rabban Gamliel, citing Hosea, that God had performed halitza on Israel and abandoned them.
19.turn: Rabban Gamliel pointed out the verse says 'from them', meaning Israel withdrew from God.
19.outcome: He called the heretic a fool and showed such a halitza has no force.
19.summary: A heretic told Rabban Gamliel that God had 'removed His shoe' from Israel, as a brother-in-law does to a widow, so the bond was over. Rabban Gamliel called him a fool: the verse says 'from them', so it is Israel who did the removing. A halitza performed by the widow's side on the brothers has no legal effect, so the bond stands.

20.event: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna, who asked to meet him.
20.turn: Rav Huna saw Rav Hamnuna's head was uncovered and learned it was because he was unmarried.
20.outcome: Rav Huna turned away and told him not to see his face again until he married.
20.summary: Rav Hisda kept telling Rav Huna what a great man Rav Hamnuna was, so Rav Huna asked to have him sent over. When he arrived, Rav Huna noticed he was not wearing the scholar's head-cloth and asked why; Rav Hamnuna said it was because he was not married. Rav Huna turned his face away and told him not to come before him again until he had a wife.
